data.title: Hainburg – Braunsberg, a Celtic hillfort at the Hungarian Gate
data.excerpt: The isolated 376-metre hill of Braunsberg above Austrian Hainburg carries one of the three Celtic hillforts of the Hungarian Gate, alongside Devín and the oppidum on the Bratislava castle hill. A reconstructed section of palisade and watchtower marks its summit; the timber-and-earth rampart is dated to the 2nd century BC, and the hillfort was destroyed in the first decades of our era.

children.text: The hill of Braunsberg, situated in the Austrian town of Hainburg, is one of three Celtic hillforts located in the area of the so-called Hungarian Gate. This prominent, 376 metres high isolated hill is noticed by every visitor passing through this picturesque Austrian town in the immediate vicinity of Bratislava. On its summit your eye is caught from afar by a reconstructed section of the palisade and of the watchtower. Prominent Slovak archaeologists also took part in building the reconstruction of the defences. Barely 2 kilometres north-east of Braunsberg the hillfort of Devín rose in the La Tène period. The third – and the most important hillfort at that time – was the oppidum on the Bratislava castle hill and in its suburbium, which evidently had a central function. It is assumed that the hillforts were built 2000 years ago by the Celtic tribe of the Boii.
The first archaeological excavation at Braunsberg was carried out in 1931 and continued in the following decades until the 1990s.

The oldest occupation, which was significantly represented at the hillfort, can be observed in the Hallstatt period (the Early Iron Age) – approximately in the 7th to 6th centuries BC, when an important centre is assumed here. So far, however, it has not been possible to identify remains of defences from this period. The rich burial mounds built in this period in the immediate vicinity of the hillfort testify to the importance of the site at that time.

In 1988 the defences of the hillfort were precisely surveyed and analysed. It was established that in the southern and western parts of the hillfort there stood a timber-and-earth rampart approximately 1.5 m high. In the northern and eastern parts, on the gently sloping side of the hill, the defences without the palisade were about 3 m high. The rampart is dated to the 2nd century BC. Within the defences two rows of palisade were identified, one on the crest of the rampart, the other about 2 metres in front of the rampart. In the 1930s stones were recorded, though insufficiently investigated, which evidently formed a stone facing bonded to the timber-and-earth rampart. In the period of the first decades of our era a destruction horizon is apparent on the defences, and so in this period the hillfort was evidently destroyed. In the area of the former gateway and the adjoining defences this destruction is particularly noticeable.

After this destruction of the hillfort we find, in a later period, traces of the renewal of the defences again, in the period of approximately the 4th–5th centuries, that is in the turbulent period of the fall of the Roman Empire and of the Migration Period. At that time a dry-laid stone rampart was built along the summit plateau of the hillfort, at its edge.

The Celtic occupation of the hillfort certainly included houses – semi-sunken buildings with a hearth – and storage pits, which were discovered during the excavation in Hainburg in the vicinity of the hillfort. Graphite sherd material was also recorded in them, which allows the houses to be dated to the period of the 1st century BC.

It appears that the area of the Hungarian Gate was already in the Early Iron Age an important crossroads of significant ancient routes – the Amber Road and the so-called Danube route, which were of key importance for the long-distance trade of that time. The importance of this crossroads is underlined by the building of the three hillforts mentioned, whose task was evidently, among other things, also to control long-distance trade and to profit from it.
